docs.title: Bootleg Catalog Manager
docs.text: Bootleg Catalog Manager is a local-first desktop application for cataloging live recordings and building custom PDF/XLSX exports. The catalog is stored in SQLite, there is no cloud component and no telemetry. A set of recordings is saved as a .bootleg session file, and exports are built from user-editable layout templates rather than fixed report formats. FFprobe supplies the technical metadata, and the application never modifies your media files.

docs.title: Guides
docs.text:
• Installation — install on Windows with the installer, or run from source on Linux and macOS; FFmpeg and FFprobe setup.
  • First steps — create a session, add recordings, choose a layout, and run your first export.
  • Audio recordings — add a single audio file or an album folder as one entry; screenshots do not apply to audio.
  • Layouts — write layout templates with field markers and inline formatting.
  • Screenshots — generate screenshots with FFmpeg, pick up images stored next to your media, or attach your own.
  • Rips and multi-part recordings — add DVD and Blu-ray rip folders as a single entry, and combine multi-part recordings.
  • Export — produce a PDF catalog or an XLSX spreadsheet.
  • Settings — configure the FFmpeg and FFprobe paths and the suggestion lists.
  • Troubleshooting — solutions for common problems.

docs.title: Download
docs.text:
Pre-built installers are available on the Releases page.

Download the latest release

The installer is currently Windows-only. Linux and macOS users can run the app from source — see Installation.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Windows 10 or newer (for the installer)
  • FFmpeg and FFprobe, installed separately — see Installation
  • Python 3.12 or newer and PySide6 are only needed for the source install path, not for the installer

Pre-built installer for Windows; Linux and macOS supported via source install.

docs.title: Audio recordings
docs.text: Audio recordings live in the same session as video recordings and are driven by the same layouts. The difference is how they are added and what they can show: an audio entry has no video frames, so screenshots never apply to it.

docs.title: Adding an audio recording
docs.text:
Use + Add Audio Recording… in the toolbar, next to + Add Video Recording…. A dialog asks whether the source is a single file or a folder:

  • Single file… — pick one audio file (FLAC, MP3, M4A, AAC, OGG, Opus, WAV, WMA, AIFF, APE, or ALAC). It is probed with FFprobe and added the same way a video file is.
  • Folder… — pick an album folder. Every audio file directly inside the folder becomes ONE entry (subfolders are ignored): the tracks are read in sorted order, their durations are summed into the entry's duration, and the first track's audio parameters stand for the whole album. The folder path is the recording's source.

Both routes end in the same add dialog as video, where the archival fields are filled in by hand.

docs.title: Screenshots
docs.text: Audio entries have no frames to capture, so [Screenshot:N] resolves to nothing for them — the token draws no images in the preview and in every export. Video recordings are unaffected; see Screenshots.

docs.title: Layouts
docs.text:
The same layout markers work for audio:

  • {Duration} — the single file's length, or the summed track durations of an album
  • {Audio Codec}, {Sample Rate}, {Audio Bitrate}, {Audio Channels} — read from the file, or from the first track of an album
  • [Venue], [Show], [Year], and the other archival fields behave as they do for video

A session can mix video and audio entries without changing the layout. See Layouts for the marker syntax, and First steps for where adding recordings fits in the workflow.

docs.title: Export
docs.text: A session exports to two formats: PDF and XLSX. Both are driven by the same layout (see Layouts), so the fields and screenshots in the export are the ones the layout asks for.

docs.title: PDF
docs.text:
The PDF export renders the session as pages: a header band, one block per recording with the fields in layout order, inline formatting, optional screenshots at [Screenshot:N] positions, and a footer band. Header and footer bands can carry text and optional logo images.

Page size (A4, Letter, A3), orientation (portrait or landscape), and custom margins are part of the page setup, so the same layout can produce a small hand list or a full-page catalog.

Use the PDF when the catalog is meant to be read or printed as a document.

docs.title: XLSX
docs.text:
The XLSX export writes the recordings as spreadsheet rows, one row per recording, with the layout's fields as columns. It is meant for further processing: sorting, filtering, or reusing the data in another tool.

Use the XLSX when the catalog is meant to be worked with as data rather than read as pages.

docs.title: Sessions
docs.text: File → Save As… writes the session itself as a .bootleg file — a ZIP archive holding the layout, the recordings, and any manually attached screenshots. It is self-contained: with the media files it references, it opens unchanged on another machine. File → Open… or the startup "Continue a recent session" flow loads one again.

docs.title: If an export fails
docs.text: The two formats fail differently, and the usual causes are listed under Troubleshooting — in particular the latin-1 limit of the PDF writer, which does not apply to the XLSX export.

docs.text:

  • Screenshots — the images embedded in either format

docs.title: First steps
docs.text: This page walks through the basic sequence: open the app, create a session, add a recording, pick a layout, and export.

docs.title: Open the application
docs.text:
Open Bootleg Catalog Manager from the Start Menu (Windows) or from wherever you installed it. See Installation if it is not installed yet.

??? note "Running from source"

```bash
python -m bootleg_catalog.app.main
```

On start, the application offers a choice between creating a new session and continuing a recent one. Recent sessions are listed by name; choosing one loads it directly.

docs.title: Create a session
docs.text:
A session is the unit of work: it holds the recordings you are cataloging together with the layout used to export them. Sessions are saved as .bootleg files (see Export).

When you create a new session, you are asked for a display name. The name identifies the session in the recent-session list.

docs.title: Add a recording
docs.text:
Add recordings by scanning a folder for media files. The catalog reads the technical metadata with FFprobe — codecs, duration, file size, and the rest — and never modifies the media files themselves. Files already present in the session are skipped when you scan the same folder again.

Recordings can also be imported as a single entry from a disc rip folder; see Rips and multi-part recordings.

Audio recordings are added the same way, with + Add Audio Recording… — either a single audio file or a folder of tracks as one album entry; see Audio recordings.

docs.title: Pick a layout
docs.text: Every export is driven by a layout template. A default layout is provided; adjust it in the layout designer when you need a different set of fields, a different order, or screenshots at a different position. The marker syntax is described in Layouts.

docs.title: Export
docs.text: Once the session holds recordings and the layout looks right, run the export. The result is either a PDF catalog or an XLSX spreadsheet — see Export for what each format contains.

docs.title: Save the session
docs.text: Use File → Save As… to write the session to a .bootleg file, and File → Open… or the startup "Continue a recent session" flow to load it again later.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: There are two ways to get the application. On Windows the quickest path is the installer; on Linux and macOS you run from source. The application itself works on all three platforms.

docs.title: Install on Windows (installer)
docs.text:
1. Open the Releases page.
  2. Download the latest BootlegCatalogManagerSetup-*.exe (the version in the filename matches the release).
  3. Run it. If Windows shows a SmartScreen warning ("Windows protected your PC"), click "More info" and then "Run anyway". The warning appears because the installer is not code-signed.
  4. Choose whether to install for the current user (no administrator rights needed) or for all users (Windows asks for administrator rights).
  5. Follow the wizard. The application is installed and a Start Menu shortcut is created.

docs.title: FFmpeg and FFprobe are still required
docs.text:
The installer does not bundle FFmpeg or FFprobe. The catalog reads technical metadata with FFprobe, and screenshots are generated with FFmpeg, so install both on Windows as well:

  • Download a release build from https://ffmpeg.org/download.html.
  • Unpack it somewhere stable, for example C:\ffmpeg.
  • Either add its bin\ folder to PATH, or set the full paths to the executables in the application's Settings after the first launch — see Settings.

docs.title: How to uninstall
docs.text: Open Windows Settings → Apps → Installed apps, select "Bootleg Catalog Manager", and choose Uninstall.

docs.title: Run from source (Linux, macOS, and developers)
docs.text: The steps are the same on every platform; only the activation command differs.

docs.title: 1. Clone the repository
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/fca-a/bootleg-catalog-manager.git
cd bootleg-catalog-manager

docs.title: 2. Create a virtual environment
docs.text:
WindowsLinux / macOS 
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate

python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

docs.title: 3. Install the dependencies
docs.text:
pip install -e ".[dev]"

The dev extra installs the test runner and PyInstaller alongside the application's own dependencies (PySide6, fpdf2, openpyxl, Pillow).

docs.title: FFmpeg and FFprobe
docs.text:
The catalog reads technical metadata with FFprobe, and screenshots are generated with FFmpeg. Both tools must either be available on PATH or be configured in the application:

  • Linux: install the distribution package, for example sudo apt install ffmpeg.
  • macOS: install with Homebrew, brew install ffmpeg.
  • Windows: download a release build, unpack it, and add its bin directory to PATH.

If the executables are not on PATH, set their full paths in the settings dialog after the first start — see Settings.

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
python -m bootleg_catalog.app.main

Continue with First steps.

docs.title: Building a standalone executable (optional)
docs.text:
pyinstaller bootleg-catalog-manager.spec

The executable is written under dist/. Helper scripts for the same build exist as scripts/build.bat (Windows) and scripts/build.sh (Linux and macOS).

docs.title: Layouts
docs.text: Layouts are text templates that drive both the PDF and the XLSX export. Every line of a layout becomes a line of the output, with the field markers replaced by the recording's values.

docs.title: Marker families
docs.text:
There are two marker families, and they carry different meaning:

  • {FieldName} for technical fields, for example {Duration}, {Resolution}, {Video Codec}
  • [FieldName] for archival fields, for example [Show], [Venue], [Year], [Trade Status]

Technical fields hold what FFprobe read from the file; archival fields hold what you cataloged by hand.

docs.title: Inline formatting
docs.text:
Formatting markers wrap a run of text inside a line:

  • **bold** for bold text
  • *italic* for italic text
  • ==highlight== for a highlighted run
  • [mark=#RRGGBB]text[/mark] for a custom highlight color
  • [color=#RRGGBB]text[/color] for a text color

The highlight and text color markers take a hex color with a leading #.

docs.title: Screenshots in a layout
docs.text: [Screenshot:N] places N screenshots (1-20) wherever the layout calls for them. The size, spacing, borders, and alignment come from the screenshot settings in the page setup; see Screenshots.

docs.title: Page setup
docs.text: The page setup controls the paper size (A4, Letter, A3), orientation (portrait or landscape), and custom margins. Header and footer bands can carry text and optional logo images.

docs.title: Background colors
docs.text:
The page setup dialog also has a Backgrounds group with five colors, one per area of the page. Any of the five can be left unset, which keeps the export's default — a white page with no fills:

  • Page background — the whole page, behind everything
  • Header background — the band across the top margin, behind the header text
  • Footer background — the band across the bottom margin, behind the footer text
  • Body background — the content column between the two bands
  • Screenshot background — the fill behind each image placed by [Screenshot:N]

Each row shows its current color as a swatch; clicking it opens a color picker, and clearing it returns the area to unset. The colors are part of the layout, so they travel with the session file, and the export preview shows them before the PDF is written.

docs.title: Trade Status
docs.text: [Trade Status] is a free-text archival field for whether the recording can be traded. It ships with two default suggestions: NFT (Not For Trade) and NFTF (Not For Trade Forever). Any value can be typed — the suggestions are a starting point, not a fixed list. The suggestion list is not yet editable in the settings dialog; that is planned for a future release.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
{Date} — [Show]
{Duration} at [Venue], [Location]
==[Year]==  [Video Codec]
[Screenshot:2]

For each recording this prints the date and show name, a line with the duration, venue, and location, the year highlighted together with the video codec, and finally two screenshots.

Layouts are edited in the layout designer, which previews the result as you type. See First steps for where the designer fits in the workflow.

docs.title: Rips and multi-part recordings
docs.text: A disc rip is a folder of many small files — .VOB and .m2ts pieces, plus the supporting files of the disc structure. The catalog imports such a folder as a single recording entry rather than one entry per file.

docs.title: Rip folders
docs.text:
Two folder layouts are detected automatically:

  • VIDEO_TS — the file structure of a DVD
  • BDMV — the file structure of a Blu-ray

When one of these folders is imported, all of its files become one entry, so a ripped disc shows up in the catalog the way it was released.

docs.title: Format label
docs.text:
During the import you pick a format label for the entry:

  • DVD
  • VIDEO_TS
  • VOB + Small files
  • VOB with Smalls

The label records how the rip is laid out, which keeps the catalog readable when a collection mixes full-disc rips with loose VOB files.

docs.title: Duration is entered by hand
docs.text: FFprobe cannot read a full disc structure starting from its first VOB file, so the total duration of a rip folder is not available automatically. The import asks for it instead, and you type it in.

docs.title: Multi-part recordings
docs.text: Some recordings span two files — a disc change, or a split transfer. Up to two files can be combined into a single entry, so the recording is cataloged once with both of its parts instead of twice.

docs.title: Screenshots
docs.text:
Screenshots are images attached to a recording. They are placed into the export by the [Screenshot:N] layout token (see Layouts); the number in the token is the maximum per recording, from 1 to 20.

There are three ways to get screenshots into a session. They can be mixed: an automatically generated set can be extended with your own images, and either can be reordered afterwards.

docs.title: Automatic generation with FFmpeg
docs.text: The Screenshot Manager can generate screenshots directly from a recording's video file with FFmpeg. You choose how many frames to capture, and the application extracts them at evenly spaced points of the recording and stores them with the session. Generation needs the recording's duration, so it is available once the file has been probed — see Installation if FFmpeg is not set up yet.

docs.title: Sidecar images next to the media file
docs.text: Images stored next to a media file are picked up automatically when the file is added to the session. If a folder already contains frames exported by another tool, no manual step is needed; place them beside the video files before scanning.

docs.title: Manual attachment in the Screenshot Manager
docs.text: You can attach your own images to any recording, remove ones you do not want, and reorder them. Order matters: the first screenshot in the manager is the first one placed by [Screenshot:N] in the export.

docs.title: Where they end up
docs.text:
Both export formats include the session's screenshots — in the PDF at the token position, and in the XLSX export as embedded images. See Export.

Screenshots are saved inside the .bootleg session file together with the recordings, so a session stays self-contained on another machine: copy the session file and the media files, and the images travel with them.

docs.title: Related pages
docs.text:
• Layouts — placing [Screenshot:N] in a template
  • Settings — configuring the FFmpeg used for generation

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: The settings dialog holds two groups of values: the media tool paths and the suggestion lists.

docs.title: FFmpeg and FFprobe paths
docs.text:
The catalog reads technical metadata with FFprobe, and screenshots are generated with FFmpeg. By default the application expects both on PATH, which is the usual state on Linux and macOS after a package-manager install.

If they live somewhere else — for example an unpacked release build on Windows — set the full path to each executable in the settings. The application then uses the configured executables for new scans and for new screenshot generation.

See Installation for where to obtain the tools, and Screenshots for what FFmpeg is used for.

docs.title: Suggestion lists
docs.text:
Three fields come with editable suggestion lists:

  • Type — what kind of recording it is
  • Source — where the recording came from
  • Quality — how the recording rates

Each list ships with sensible defaults. The lists are editable: add the labels you use for your own collection, and remove ones you never pick. The suggestions offered when you catalog a recording follow the lists as you edited them, so the catalog stays consistent across sessions without typing the same labels repeatedly.

Trade Status is a fourth field with suggestions. It ships with two defaults, NFT (Not For Trade) and NFTF (Not For Trade Forever), and accepts any typed value. The Trade Status list is not yet editable in the settings dialog; that is planned for a future release.

docs.title: Related pages
docs.text:

  • Screenshots — what FFmpeg generates once configured
  • Troubleshooting — what to check when the tools are not found

docs.title: FFmpeg or FFprobe is not found
docs.text:
Symptom: scanning a folder produces no technical metadata, or screenshot generation refuses to start.

The application looks for both tools on PATH. Either add the directory containing them to PATH, or set the full executable paths in the settings dialog — see Settings and Installation. Restart the scan after changing the paths.

docs.title: Screenshots are missing from an export
docs.text:
Check the following, in order:

  • The recording actually has screenshots — open the Screenshot Manager for it. See Screenshots for the three ways to get them into a session.
  • The layout contains a [Screenshot:N] token where you expect them. Without the token no screenshot is placed, whatever the recording holds. See Layouts.
  • The images are attached to the recording you expect. Reordering in the Screenshot Manager changes which image takes which slot.

docs.title: A legacy .bootleg file will not open
docs.text:
A .bootleg file is a ZIP archive holding the layout, the recordings, and the attached screenshots. A file written by a much older version may predate the current session format and fail to load.

There is no in-place conversion. Create a new session and add the recordings again; the media files themselves are never modified, so nothing is lost but the cataloging work.

docs.title: PDF export fails on non-latin-1 characters
docs.text:
The PDF export fails when the layout or a field contains characters outside the latin-1 range — for example Cyrillic, Greek, or CJK text. Accented characters within latin-1 (such as é or ñ) are fine.

Two ways out:

  • Export the session as XLSX instead. The spreadsheet format is not limited to latin-1 and keeps every character — see Export.
  • Replace the offending characters in the field values or in the layout text with latin-1 equivalents.
